stories.headline: Wall Street opens September in the red: S&P 7,631, Dow −419 as oil and yields climb
stories.dek: Nasdaq −1%. Big Tech led the slide after fresh U.S. strikes on Iran.
stories.caveman: Tuesday was a rough first day of September. The S&P 500 fell 54.67 points, or 0.7%, to 7,631.47. The Dow lost 419.02 points, or 0.8%, to 52,766.88. The Nasdaq dropped 271.11 points, or 1%, to 26,099.77. Traders pointed at two things: oil jumping after new U.S. strikes on Iran, and the 10-year Treasury yield rising to about 4.79%. Higher oil makes people fear inflation. Higher bond yields make borrowing cost more, which often hurts stock prices — especially big tech names like Nvidia and Amazon. For the year the S&P is still up about 11.5%. Next big U.S. clues: jobs later this week and the Fed on Sept. 15–16.
stories.why_it_matters: Taipei morning screens track U.S. futures. A soft Wall Street open plus hotter oil hits chip exporters and shipping costs.
stories.camps: Bulls say the year-to-date gain is still solid. Hawks say oil + yields mean the Fed stays tough. Renters and mortgage shoppers feel the yield first.

A U.S. stock index heavy on tech companies.
The interest rate on a government bond. When it rises, loans and mortgages often get pricier.
Prices going up across many things you buy.

stories.headline: Oil settles Tuesday: WTI $90.22, Brent $94.65 after new U.S.–Iran strikes
stories.dek: Both jumped more than $4 a barrel — five-week highs. Hormuz risk is back in the price.
stories.caveman: Crude had a sharp Tuesday. U.S. oil (WTI) rose $4.46, or 5.2%, to settle at $90.22 a barrel — first close above $90 in more than a month. Brent, the global marker, rose $4.16, or 4.6%, to $94.65. That was the highest close for WTI since July 23 and for Brent since July 24. Why? New U.S. air strikes on Iran, plus fear that fighting could block more ships near the Strait of Hormuz. Two tankers were already reported hit leaving that waterway. Traders are pricing war risk, not a sudden loss of wells. Pump prices and Asian import bills feel that premium first.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan imports almost all its oil. A Hormuz scare raises freight, insurance, and gasoline costs even if barrels still exist.
stories.camps: Energy traders say transit risk is real. Doves say tit-for-tat hits often fade. Ship crews and drivers pay the insurance first.

terms.explain: The main U.S. oil price. Quoted in dollars per barrel.
The main global oil price. Many Asian cargoes track it.
A narrow waterway by Iran and Oman. A big share of world oil shipping passes near here.
The official end-of-day futures price.

stories.headline: 10-year Treasury yield hits ~4.79%, highest since Jan 2025, as hike bets rise
stories.dek: CME FedWatch ~68% chance of a Sept. 16 quarter-point hike. Jobs and CPI still ahead.
stories.caveman: U.S. government bond prices fell again Tuesday, so yields rose. The 10-year Treasury yield traded near 4.79% — about a 19-month high, last seen around January 2025. The 2-year also climbed toward about 4.39%. Markets read hotter oil and fresh Middle East fighting as inflation risk. CME FedWatch put roughly a 68% chance the Fed raises rates by a quarter point on Sept. 16 (odds were far lower before Chair Kevin Warsh spoke at Jackson Hole). A higher 10-year yield often pushes up mortgage and car-loan rates. Watch August jobs and the next CPI print before the Fed meeting.
stories.why_it_matters: When U.S. yields jump, global money can shift, the dollar can firm, and growth stocks — including Asia tech — often wobble.
stories.camps: Hawks say sticky inflation needs tighter money. Doves say war-driven oil is not the same as an overheating economy. Homebuyers feel  the loan rate either way.

terms.explain: A 10-year U.S. government bond. Its yield is a benchmark for many loans.
A CME tool that turns futures prices into odds the Fed will hike, hold, or cut.
Raising the policy rate by 0.25 percentage points.
Consumer Price Index — a common U.S. inflation scorecard.

stories.headline: U.S. diesel futures hit a 52-month high; crack spread near a record ~$107
stories.dek: Reuters: diesel up ~51% in 10 weeks as Middle East and Russia refinery strains bite.
stories.caveman: It is not only crude oil. U.S. diesel futures jumped to a 52-month high on Tuesday after climbing about 51% over the past 10 weeks, Reuters reported. The diesel crack spread — the gap between diesel and crude that shows refining profit — ran near a record around $107 a barrel on LSEG data. Why so hot? Refinery trouble in places like the Middle East and Russia, plus war risk on shipping, makes middle distillates (truck fuel, some heating fuel) scarce. That hits freight, food trucking, and farm costs. Crude can rise; diesel can rise even faster.
stories.why_it_matters: Diesel moves the real economy — trucks, ships, farms. A spike shows up in store shelves and shipping bills.
stories.camps: Refiners like fat crack spreads. Truckers and grocers hate them. Policymakers fear diesel more than gasoline for inflation headlines.

terms.explain: Fuel for many trucks, buses, ships, and some heaters. Different from gasoline.
The money gap between crude oil and refined fuels like diesel. Wide spread = fat refining margin.
Fuels in the middle of the refining barrel — diesel, jet fuel, heating oil.
London Stock Exchange Group — a big market-data company.

stories.headline: OpenAI to Apple: trade-secret fight is 'a mess of Apple's own making'
stories.dek: Court filing denies theft, blames iCloud habits and rushed exits. Apple still waves MacBook forensics.
stories.caveman: OpenAI fired back. In a late Monday filing in San Jose federal court (covered Tuesday), the ChatGPT maker said Apple failed to show stolen secrets and called the dispute 'a mess of Apple's own making.' OpenAI says Apple pushes personal iCloud for work files, walks leavers out too fast, and then still calls ex-staff for help. Apple's side still points to forensic finds on a MacBook used by ex-Apple engineer Chang Liu, including a confidential circuit schematic. The companies say OpenAI has hired roughly 400 people from Apple for hardware work. Once partners, now courtroom rivals.
stories.why_it_matters: Two U.S. giants fighting over chips, people, and devices. The case can slow OpenAI's gadget plans and warn other poachers.
stories.camps: Apple says protect the crown jewels. OpenAI says workers may leave and California lets them. Talent teams watch every filing.

terms.explain: Know-how a company keeps private because it is worth money — designs, recipes, supply tricks.
Careful dig through a computer to see what files were opened, copied, or deleted.
Apple's online storage. Personal accounts mixed with work files can blur lines.
A judge's early order that can block a company from using certain tech while a case runs.

stories.headline: Day one as Apple CEO: John Ternus inherits AI gap, foldable in 8 days, Cook as chair
stories.dek: Hardware chief takes the wheel; first big stage is the Sept. 9 iPhone event.
stories.caveman: Tuesday was John Ternus's first official day as Apple CEO. Tim Cook, after 15 years, becomes executive chairman and will still talk to world leaders for Apple. Ternus, 51, spent ~25 years at Apple and ran hardware engineering. He inherits a huge company that still trails rivals in generative AI, plus a Google Gemini licensing deal he did not negotiate, and a foldable iPhone Ultra expected at the Sept. 9 'Surprise and shine' event — about a week into the job. Johny Srouji steps up on hardware. Markets will judge Ternus first by that keynote, not by memos.
stories.why_it_matters: Apple sets the tone for phones, chips, and suppliers from Taiwan to India. A new CEO can shift product bets and factory plans.
stories.camps: Fans want a product-obsessed boss. Critics say AI lag is the real test. Cook staying as chair softens the handoff — or muddies it.

terms.explain: Chief executive officer — the top day-to-day boss.
Board role that can still guide strategy and politics without running daily ops.
Software that writes text, makes images, or answers questions by predicting patterns.
A phone with a screen that bends so it opens like a small tablet.

stories.image_alt: John Ternus and Tim Cook related Apple leadership coverage

stories.headline: iPhone Ultra leaks, day-of: MagSafe in, dual launch with Pros, crease 'mostly' tamed
stories.dek: Gurman to Tom's Guide: 5.5" cover / 7.8" inner, latest Pro chip + modem; no long delay expected.
stories.caveman: Fresh foldable crumbs landed Tuesday. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman told Tom's Guide (via 9to5Mac) that MagSafe wireless charging is planned for Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Ultra. Specs still point to about a 5.5-inch cover screen and 7.8-inch inner screen, plus the latest Apple Pro chip and modem. Multitasking should feel more iPad-like, with drag-and-drop between apps. Gurman said he would be surprised if Ultra missed launching with the new Pro phones — not a late-fall slip. The crease will not vanish, but Apple aims to match or beat new Samsung foldables. Sept. 9 is the reveal stage.
stories.why_it_matters: A real Apple foldable would shake the phone market and the parts chain — displays, hinges, glass — that Taiwan and Korea supply.
stories.camps: Believers say Apple ships when ready. Skeptics say foldables still scratch and crease. Accessory makers already sketch MagSafe wallets.

terms.explain: Apple's magnetic charging and accessory ring on the phone's back.
The faint fold line in the middle of a bending screen.
The radio chip that talks to cell towers for 5G and calls.
Two products going on sale around the same day.

stories.headline: Hot Chips: Microsoft lifts the hood on Maia 200, its homemade AI inference chip
stories.dek: TSMC 3nm, ~750W, 6× HBM stacks, all-Ethernet rack scale — aimed at Azure, not a Nvidia clone.
stories.caveman: At Hot Chips 2026 on Tuesday, Microsoft gave its deepest look yet at Maia 200 — the company's second-generation custom AI accelerator for Azure cloud. ServeTheHome notes a TSMC 3-nanometer chip, about 140 billion transistors, six HBM3e memory stacks (~7 TB/s), and a ~750-watt power draw. Microsoft stresses software-defined dataflow and all-Ethernet networking so racks stay simpler to run. The pitch: more tokens per watt for Copilot-style chat and agent work, and less total dependence on Nvidia GPUs. Other giants (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium, Meta MTIA) are on the same homemade-chip path.
stories.why_it_matters: If cloud giants bake their own AI chips, Nvidia's pricing power and Taiwan foundry bookings both shift.
stories.camps: Microsoft says efficiency wins. Nvidia fans say GPUs still rule training. Chip investors watch who can actually ship at scale.

terms.explain: A special chip built to run AI math fast, not a general laptop CPU.
Using a finished AI model to answer questions — not the expensive training step.
High Bandwidth Memory — super-fast stacked memory stuck next to an AI chip.
A yearly conference where companies show chip designs.

stories.image_alt: Microsoft Maia 200 AI accelerator hardware hero shot

stories.headline: U.S. launches new strikes on IRGC sites in Iran; Tehran fires back, Trump warns harder hits
stories.dek: CENTCOM: radar, air defense, mine-laying, maritime targets. Oil and markets jolted.
stories.caveman: The quiet month broke. On Tuesday U.S. Central Command said American forces struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets in Iran — air defenses, radars, maritime gear, mine-laying kit, and communications. Washington tied the raids to IRGC moves against shipping near Hormuz and against U.S. troops. President Trump called the strikes 'large and powerful' and warned that if Iran hits back harder, the U.S. will hit 'much harder.' Iranian forces claimed missile replies, including toward a U.S. site in Jordan; Iran also said a strike hit a wedding gathering in Sirik. Oil jumped; stocks fell. The wider war that cooled after July is hot again.
stories.why_it_matters: A wider U.S.–Iran fight moves oil, shipping insurance, and U.S. politics in one day.
stories.camps: Hawks say punish mine threats. Critics fear civilian harm and spiral. Gulf neighbors brace for debris and drones.

terms.explain: Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps — a powerful Iranian military force.
U.S. Central Command — the U.S. military HQ for the Middle East region.
Chokepoint waterway for a large share of seaborne oil.
When each side answers with a bigger punch, and the fight grows.

stories.headline: SCO Bishkek Declaration condemns strikes on Iran and 'unilateral' sanctions
stories.dek: Xi, Putin, Modi, Sharif among signers. Bloc backs Iran's peaceful nuclear rights under NPT.
stories.caveman: In Kyrgyzstan's capital Bishkek, Shanghai Cooperation Organisation leaders signed a joint Bishkek Declaration on Tuesday. The text condemns military strikes on Iran, offers condolences over Iranian deaths including the late supreme leader, and opposes 'unilateral coercive measures' — code for Western sanctions — that clash with UN and WTO rules. Members also backed Iran's right to peaceful nuclear work under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The SCO mixes China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Iran, and Central Asian states. Analysts noted tough Iran language and little on Ukraine. Energy cooperation talk rose while Hormuz routes stay risky.
stories.why_it_matters: A big Eurasian club just publicly sided with Iran on war and sanctions — a diplomatic signal to Washington and Brussels.
stories.camps: SCO states call it defending sovereignty. Western officials call it cover for Russia and Iran. India still balances ties with the U.S.

terms.explain: Shanghai Cooperation Organisation — a regional club led in practice by China and Russia.
Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty — deal that limits who may have nuclear weapons and protects peaceful nuclear power.
Penalties one country or bloc puts on another without a full UN vote.
Capital of Kyrgyzstan; host of this SCO summit.

stories.headline: Zelensky: 'September could change a lot' after call with Witkoff and Kushner
stories.dek: Says U.S. envoys prepare Russia talks and a Ukraine visit; intel still shows Putin wants war.
stories.caveman: On Tuesday evening Ukraine time, President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had just spoken with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, envoys for U.S. President Trump. He called the talk detailed and said they are preparing more contact with Russia and a visit to Ukraine. Zelensky briefed them on the front and on air attacks. He also said all intelligence he sees still shows Vladimir Putin wants the war to go on — even if many Russians would accept a stop along the current line. 'September could change a lot,' he said, asking partners to push for peace while protecting lives. Earlier date-locks alone are old; this is the September pitch.
stories.why_it_matters: U.S. envoys shuttling while Russia pounds Kyiv. A real trip or real talks would move European security overnight.
stories.camps: Kyiv wants leverage and air defense. Moscow shows no rush. Trump's team sells deal-making; skeptics want proof.

terms.explain: A person sent to talk for a president or government.
The front line where the two armies face each other.
Missiles and guns that try to shoot down drones and rockets.
Steve Witkoff — a Trump point person on Ukraine–Russia talks.

stories.image_alt: Volodymyr Zelensky speaking in a formal setting

stories.headline: Modi, at SCO, urges Putin to leave 'endless war' as Kyiv counts another deadly night
stories.dek: BBC: Indian PM tells close partner Russia to move toward peace while Russian strikes kill 12 near Kyiv.
stories.caveman: On the sidelines of big-power diplomacy, India's Narendra Modi publicly urged Russia's Vladimir Putin to move 'from an endless war to an end of war,' BBC reported Tuesday — a notable line from a leader whose country still buys lots of discounted Russian oil. The plea landed as Ukraine said Russian missiles and jet-powered drones killed at least 12 people in and around Kyiv on the sixth straight day of heavy attacks. Moscow said it hit military and energy sites. The split screen is the story: SCO solidarity language on Iran in Bishkek, and a rare on-camera nudge to Putin about Ukraine.
stories.why_it_matters: India sits between Washington and Moscow. A public peace nudge matters even if oil trade continues.
stories.camps: Delhi says it speaks for peace. Critics say cheap oil funds the war. Kyiv welcomes any pressure on Putin.

terms.explain: Oil sold cheaper than the usual world price — a lure for buyers.
Meetings that happen next to a big summit, not on the main stage.
A drone with a jet engine — faster and harder to shoot down than slow propeller drones.

stories.image_alt: Coverage image related to Modi–Putin diplomacy and Ukraine war

stories.headline: Pardon My Book debuts PW overall No. 2 with 49,297 print copies — messy on purpose
stories.dek: Barstool podcast duo Big Cat & PFT top hardcover nonfiction; outsell Portnoy's earlier hit.
stories.caveman: Sports-podcast chaos hit the book chart. Publishers Weekly's Aug. 31 list (Circana BookScan week ended Aug. 22) has Pardon My Book by Dan 'Big Cat' Katz and Eric 'PFT Commenter' Sollenberger at No. 2 overall and No. 1 hardcover nonfiction with 49,297 print copies in week one. PW says that beats Dave Portnoy's Cancel Me If You Can debut by about 14,000 copies. The hosts brag the book is barely edited — 'telling over spelling.' Love it or hate it, that is the U.S. print market this week: a loud podcast yearbook sitting just behind quiet literary giant Theo of Golden.
stories.why_it_matters: Shows how podcast fame still prints physical books — and how Circana counts move the industry.
stories.camps: Fans call it a souvenir. Editors wince. Bookstores note it sells anyway.

terms.explain: Service that counts most U.S. print book sales for bestseller lists.
True-story / essay / memoir books in hard covers.
First week on the list.
Barstool Sports — a loud U.S. sports-media brand.

stories.headline: The Poison Daughter opens at PW No. 1 hardcover fiction / No. 4 overall (27,068)
stories.dek: Sheila Masterson's romantasy rides TikTok into Slowburn; Hulu series interest noted.
stories.caveman: Romantasy keeps eating the fiction table. The Poison Daughter by Sheila Masterson debuts at No. 1 on Publishers Weekly's hardcover fiction list and No. 4 overall with 27,068 Circana print copies (week ended Aug. 22; Aug. 31 PW). Masterson self-published earlier work; Slowburn took this title after social buzz, and PW notes Hulu interest. The book joins a crowded U.S. fantasy-romance boom. On the same overall chart, Freida McFadden's Brain Damage sits No. 3 and Allen Levi's Theo of Golden still holds No. 1 — but Poison Daughter is the new hardcover fiction story of the week.
stories.why_it_matters: Tracks what U.S. readers actually buy: romantasy and thrillers, not only prize novels.
stories.camps: TikTok readers celebrate. Literary purists grumble. Publishers hunt the next Slowburn.

terms.explain: Romance plus fantasy — love stories with magic, fae, or poison kisses.
Made-up stories sold in hard covers.
A romance publisher imprint named for slow-building chemistry — also this book's house.

stories.headline: IndieBound: Yesteryear still No. 1 (week 20); Poison Daughter is the new No. 6 Indie Next
stories.dek: Independent bookstores keep Caro Claire Burke on top; Stockett and Patchett hold strong.
stories.caveman: At U.S. indie bookstores, Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke is still No. 1 hardcover fiction on the national IndieBound list dated around Aug. 26 — week 20 on the list. The Calamity Club by Kathryn Stockett and Whistler by Ann Patchett stay near the top. The fresh move: The Poison Daughter lands as a September Indie Next Pick and shows as a new entry around No. 6 on indie lists. That split matters — chain/Circana charts love podcasts and TikTok; indies still push literary debuts and book-club novels. Same country, two taste maps.
stories.why_it_matters: IndieBound is the pulse of independent shops — often where prize buzz and book clubs start.
stories.camps: Indie booksellers champion Burke and Patchett. Mass merchants push McFadden and sports bros. Readers can ignore both and browse.

terms.explain: Bestseller list built from independent U.S. bookstores.
Monthly picks indie booksellers recommend.
Internet trend romanticizing old-fashioned housewife roles — Yesteryear's satirical spark.

stories.headline: The Nerd Reich hits PW hardcover nonfiction No. 6 as Durán warns on tech power
stories.dek: Starred PW interview book on billionaire politics sits behind Haberman/Swan's Regime Change.
stories.caveman: Not all nonfiction is podcast jokes. Gil Durán's The Nerd Reich appears at No. 6 on Publishers Weekly's hardcover nonfiction list in the Aug. 31 package, with a starred PW take calling it a sharp look at antidemocratic ideas among tech billionaires tied to Trump's second term. Durán's line, paraphrased: the world has billions of people and only thousands of billionaires — pick democracy or billionaire rule. It sits behind chart leaders like Pardon My Book and Maggie Haberman & Jonathan Swan's Regime Change. U.S. readers are buying both meme sports books and dark tech-politics books in the same week.
stories.why_it_matters: Shows a serious U.S. appetite for books that audit tech power — not only escapism.
stories.camps: Tech critics cheer. Silicon Valley shrugs. Book clubs may actually finish this one.

terms.explain: Books about real people and real events.
A critic's extra-strong recommendation in trade magazines like PW.
Haberman & Swan book on Trump's imperial presidency style — another NF chart fixture.

stories.headline: Nepal–Tibet floods: death toll passes 1,000; 4,200+ still missing; DNA ID drive
stories.dek: UN OCHA Tuesday: glacier collapse disaster enters second week. 43,000 women and girls need aid.
stories.caveman: The Himalayan flood disaster got worse on the numbers. UN aid office OCHA said Tuesday the death toll is just over 1,000, with about 4,247 people still missing after a glacier collapse on the Nepal–China border. China side reports are smaller but still deadly. Nepal police asked relatives of missing tourists for DNA and photos because many bodies are hard to identify; some areas already used mass burial with tags after morgues filled. UN Women says about 43,000 women and girls need immediate help. Red Cross teams are only now reaching some cut-off districts. Monsoon and landslide risk continue.
stories.why_it_matters: One of 2026's deadliest climate-linked disasters. Missing foreigners make it a global family crisis too.
stories.camps: Rescuers beg for speed and money. Climate scientists point at warming glaciers. Locals want water, food, and roads first.

terms.explain: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs — the UN's emergency aid traffic cop.
When a big ice mass breaks and sends floodwater, mud, and rock downhill fast.
Using genetic samples to match unnamed bodies to families.
Seasonal heavy rain pattern in South Asia.

stories.headline: WFP halves West Bank food aid: 400,000 people cut to 200,000 from September
stories.dek: Agency needs $386M more in six months for Gaza + West Bank; Gaza cash already cut 40% for some.
stories.caveman: Hunger math got crueler. On Tuesday the World Food Programme said funding gaps force it to cut West Bank food help from about 400,000 people to 200,000 starting this month — even though need has more than doubled since 2023 and roughly 900,000 West Bank residents are food insecure. Tiny cash transfers (under $20 a person per month) that acted as a lifeline will shrink. In Gaza, WFP already cut cash value 40% for hundreds of thousands in July and warns more cuts without new money. WFP wants about $386 million extra over six months for some two million hungry people across both territories.
stories.why_it_matters: Aid is a pipe, not a speech. When donors quit, families eat less — ceasefire or not.
stories.camps: WFP says prioritize the neediest. Families already skipping meals disagree with the math. Donors cite budget fatigue.

terms.explain: World Food Programme — the UN's main food-aid agency.
Not sure you can get enough safe food tomorrow.
Aid given as money or vouchers so people can buy food locally.
Palestinian territory west of the Jordan River, under Israeli occupation in large part.

stories.headline: Kyiv's sixth deadly night: at least 12 killed, including rail workers; jet drones overwhelm
stories.dek: Zelensky: ballistic missiles + jet drones. Air force says interception rates lag on new drones.
stories.caveman: Ukraine's capital woke to another body count. Officials said at least 12 people died and about 20 were hurt in overnight Russian missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and nearby towns — the sixth straight day of heavy strikes. About six of the dead were railway workers when a depot was hit. Russia said it aimed at military and energy sites. Ukraine says Moscow is flooding the sky with faster jet-powered drones that are harder to shoot down, wearing out air defenses and nerves as kids head back toward school season. Rescue crews numbered in the hundreds overnight.
stories.why_it_matters: Civilian deaths on a European capital's doorstep keep the war on the morning front page.
stories.camps: Kyiv begs for more interceptors. Moscow calls targets legitimate. EU ministers talk air defense while apartments burn.

terms.explain: A rocket that flies high then falls fast on a target.
Uncrewed aircraft with a jet engine — quicker than propeller drones.
Systems that try to destroy incoming missiles and drones.
A rail yard or warehouse where trains and gear sit.

stories.image_alt: Aftermath of strikes in Kyiv region

stories.headline: Sudan: El Obeid 'shockingly overcrowded' as new waves of displaced families arrive
stories.dek: EDGE/Save the Children: 15,000+ families since mid-July on top of 200,000 earlier; water still broken.
stories.caveman: Away from the headlines about Iran and Kyiv, Sudan's war keeps swallowing cities. Reporting dated Tuesday describes El Obeid and nearby camps as 'dire and deteriorating,' with more than 15,000 families arriving since mid-July after earlier waves above 200,000 people. Volunteers call the city shockingly overcrowded. RSF drone damage earlier wrecked water and power; many still rely on trucked water. Aid groups warn of disease risk in rainy season and of children out of school by the millions nationwide. Sudan remains one of the world's largest displacement crises — even when cameras look elsewhere.
stories.why_it_matters: Scale of suffering can be huge and still under-covered. Displacement now shapes famine and disease risk.
stories.camps: Aid workers want access and cash. Warring parties keep fighting. Neighbors host refugees with thin budgets.

terms.explain: Internally displaced person — someone forced from home who stays inside their country.
Rapid Support Forces — one main armed side in Sudan's civil war.
Major city in Sudan's North Kordofan — a hub for people fleeing nearby fighting.
Hauling drinking water by truck when pipes and wells fail.
